“Forties” is slang for the 40 ounce beer bottles that is a popular drink when you wanna get drunk real quick.

line: [Intro: James Fauntleroy] Thousand lives ago We were young, and we didn’t know We were trading our crowns for our souls Made the sacrifice, headed back to the light But be careful, don’t drown in the gold I know it glows, but it’s cold
vault_lines: We were young, and we didn't know
meaning:
The introduction to this album begins with James Fauntleroy of Cocaine 80’s singing about the adolescents of Chicago making the immature choice of joining gangs, while subsequently selling their souls to the streets. Interestingly enough, the setting of this soliloquy was a thousand years ago to symbolize how one’s childhood can seem like forever ago.

He reminds the young gang members not to get too involved with the streets, or they will never come back from such actions. He understands that the accommodations of gang life can be enticing, but you should never get yourself into something that you can’t get out of.

line: Fiends choked off of smoke, herringbones and rope
vault_lines: Fiends choked off of smoke, herringbones and rope
meaning:
He is referring to the fact that poor people in general didn’t only choke off of smoke (probably Crack). In addition, they choked off of herringbones (bad food) that they had to eat cause they were forced to eat because of their financial status. The rope refers to a sling; which means that the people were depressed, suicidal, and wanted to hang themselves.



Herringbones (left) and ropes (right) also refer to different styles of gold chains. Literally worn around the neck, the struggle to afford such luxuries is described metaphorically through choking.

In order to get that money he was after there were certain things that Common had to avoid:


Cases – as in legal court cases being placed against him which would see him go to jail.

line: I came from a place where it’s basic, but you don’t make it (Nah)
vault_lines: I came from a place where it's basic, but you don't make it (Nah)
meaning:
Lil Herb was born and raised in the area known as “Terror Town” in East Chicago. It is known for it’s high unemployment rate, and so many families have to live with the most basic of necessities to survive.

Not only that but Terror Town is also well known for it’s many gangs, such as the Black P. Stone (of which Herb is a member), and the subsequent high number of shootings has has resulted in many people’s deaths.



By “make it” Herb could also be talking about success-wise as well as survival. Herb and fellow rapper Lil Bibby are the only two notable people to have become a success from that area of Chicago.

Here Common names gangs (and one street) primarily based in his home town of Chicago, Illinois:


Almighty Black P. Stone Nation
Four CHs – Four Corner Hustlers
Almighty Vice Lord Nation

Stoney Island Av. (Major street name not a gang)



Common has rapped about the wicked Chi City and the violence it is infested with in the past.

Black Stone is not only a gang but the eastern cornerstone of the Kaaba, the ancient stone building toward which Muslims pray. He is saying have you ever heard anything religious around such a violent gang?

line: The era of Reagan,
vault_lines: The era of Reagan, the terror of Bush
meaning:
An time who’s name was bought to us by Kendrick Lamar is referring to the time Ronald Reagan was in office (1981-1989). Being that the crack-cocaine usage and distribution was at an all time high throughout most of the 80’s this made Ronald, as the US president, responsible for stopping it thus adopting the name “Ronald Reagan Era”.



In 1982 Reagan declared a War on Drugs towards the Crack Epedemic. In 1986, Reagan signed a drug enforcement bill that budgeted $1.7 billion to fund the War on Drugs and specified a mandatory minimum penalty for drug offenses.



Maybe Juelz Santana could tell you a little more about the 80’s

The hustlers in this case were the ones setting trends and examples for the rest of the neighborhood, especially those most affiliated with them.



Some word play here, repeating fed twice in this line with both times delivering a different meaning.  The street hustlers dropped knowledge (or fed) to the younger up coming ones about the terrors of hustling such as being caugh by the feds (slang for police).

line: Small crib, big fam’, Mom was working, Granny raised us (Raised us) No food in the ’frigerator, I was banging, pulling capers—that’s real shit (Real shit)
vault_lines: Small crib, big fam', Mom was working, Granny raised us (Raised us)
meaning:
Lil Herb details the hard life that he grew up with. He had a small house but a large family, meaning he probably had to share a room with siblings.

Because his dad wasn’t around, his mother had to keep the family afloat. She was always out late working, so his grandmother was the one who spent the time with the kids.

Because they were living in poverty there was never enough food to feed everyone, so Lil Herb took matters into his own hands. He joined a gang and started robbing places to get some extra money just so that his family could survive.

line: Used to post up on that strip, I looked like a street sign (I’m out here)

Before the recent surge in violence on the streets, Lil Herb could hang out on the block for however long he wanted to. He would be there so often that he was like a stop sign: he wasn’t going anywhere.



Anther similarity between Herb and the stop sign is that Herb’s gang NLMB wears red clothing, so he would wear red while standing on the block.

line: Ain’t nobody stop the violence, why my city keep lying? (They keep lying)
vault_lines: Ain't nobody stop the violence, why my city keep lying? (They keep lying)
meaning:
Lil Herb is appalled by the massive amount of murder that he sees on the streets of Chicago.

The aforementioned groups are doing nothing to stop it, and instead are often glorifying and perpetuating gang violence.

For instance, in the song Aimed At You, Chief Keef raps:

“On that gangbanging shit, this is what I do nigga”

In the song Lil Niggaz, Lil Durk raps:

“You a lil nigga and I’m a big dog
You can die quick, nigga, only one call”

These are just a few examples out of many. Lil Herb doesn’t understand why people in his city continue to lie about what they do when in the end it just continues the endless cycle of gun violence.
